newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Telekom not affected by foreign buys.
newsitem.headline: Telekom not affected by foreign buys.

text.p: Malaysian state-run telephone company Telekom Malaysia Bhd's investments overseas are unlikely to affect its domestic earnings, Energy, Telecommunications and Posts Minister Leo Moggie said on Monday.

Speaking after a Telekom function on Labuan island, located off the coast of Borneo, Moggie told Reuters the government has ensured that Telekom's investments in Malaysia were protected while it explored overseas to secure future earnings.
"We take care and make sure that within the country, Telekom has investments (protected)," he said when asked if Telekom was ignoring the domestic market in favour of overseas ventures.
Later, Telekom chief executive Mohamed Said Mohamed Ali told reporters that the company has sufficient resources to back its investments.
"We can cope with what we have at the present moment and in future I think we won't make any investments unless we have adequate resources," he said.
There has been a surge in Telekom's overseas investments recently. Last week, it signed a deal to buy a 20.12 percent stake in Thai telephone firm Samart Corp Plc for $71.5 million.
"I think we can get dividend in Samart which will justify our investment," he said.
Telekom is also bidding for privatisation deals in Kenya and Zimbabwe, the chief executive had said last week.
Telekom recently bought a 12 percent stake in South Africa's Telkom for 504.4 million ringgit.

"Most of our overseas investments have been small, $10-15 million. It is only in South Africa that they have invested a big sum," said Mohamed Said, adding that the company was sure of good returns from the investment.
The Malaysian company has also invested in joint ventures in India, Bangladesh, Cambodia and central Asian countries which were former Soviet republics.
"We need to take opportunities because we are not talking about this year only. Telecommunications is not limited to one place, but is more global," Moggie said.
"The trend internationally is that companies are tying up with companies from other countries. We have to be sensitive to that," the minister said.
But, when asked if these investments were going to make Telekom tight on cash, Moggie said, "not at the moment."
"Our most important (investment) will be in Malaysia, especially in the Malaysian network," Mohamed Said said.
"This year we are going to invest 3.5 billion ringgit in networks in Malaysia. And we have the cash and the financial facilities," he told reporters.
